content: Stakeholders from 43 countries, including 20 high-income and 23 lowand middle-income nations, strongly supported targeted testing for specific populations. Over 85% endorsed testing blood donors, 75% supported testing children born to mothers with hepatitis B virus (HBV), 65% prioritized individuals living with HIV, and 78% emphasized testing pregnant women. Testing was also supported for men who have sex with men (MSM) and sex workers (45% each), prisoners (25%), and individuals with chronic illnesses (approximately 25%). However, only one-third of respondents supported general population testing for HBV. A systematic review and meta-analysis of hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing approaches, including general population and targeted testing, was limited by the small number of studies and the variability in settings, populations, and outcomes. Consequently, a narrative review was conducted, incorporating recent systematic reviews of HCV seroprevalence. Three main testing strategies were evaluated: (i) routine testing across the general population, (ii) targeted testing for high-risk groups, and (iii) routine testing within specific birth cohorts. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low, with most studies originating from Europe and the United States, and very few from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Fourteen studies assessed general population testing, 13 focused on people who inject drugs (PWID) and sexually transmitted disease (STD) clinics, three evaluated blood transfusion recipients, one studied HIV-infected MSM, two examined testing among pregnant women, and two targeted other populations. Targeted testing for PWID, prisoners, and HIV-infected MSM was cost-effective in all settings, even when studies assumed poor follow-up rates, limited therapy access, and high reinfection risks. Higher treatment rates enhanced population impact and cost-effectiveness. Among prisoners, focusing on those with a history of injection drug use improved cost-effectiveness. For HIV-positive MSM, cost-effectiveness depended on effective linkage to therapy and retention in care. Birth cohort testing, targeting specific age or demographic groups with higher HCV prevalence, was shown to be cost-effective in studies from the US and Portugal compared to risk-based screening. Routine general population testing was generally not cost-effective, except in high-prevalence settings. Most cost-effectiveness studies were based on older interferon-based treatments rather than newer direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapies. Only one cost-effectiveness study was conducted in an LMIC, specifically in Egypt, which has a high disease prevalence. Routine testing was cost-effective even with older treatment regimens. The optimal testing strategy for HCV depends on a country’s unique epidemic profile. Most countries exhibit mixed epidemic patterns, combining elements of high-risk behavior-related infections, birth cohort epidemics, and generalized population epidemics. Testing strategies should be tailored to these profiles to maximize diagnosis rates. Targeted testing in high-risk groups, such as PWID, MSM, prisoners, HIV-infected individuals, and sex workers, was cost-effective across all settings. Birth cohort testing is likely cost-effective in most settings, especially where unsafe medical practices or blood transfusions were common in the past. Routine general population screening is generally not cost-effective outside high-prevalence settings. Community-based testing approaches, including door-to-door campaigns, mobile outreach, and testing in workplaces, parks, and educational institutions, can increase testing uptake and early diagnosis. These methods are particularly effective in reaching first-time testers, individuals who rarely use clinical services, and asymptomatic individuals. However, challenges include ensuring confidentiality, addressing stigma, and providing access to follow-up care. Community-based testing is resource-intensive but can be cost-effective in LMICs, as demonstrated by a study in West Africa. Facility-based testing offers opportunities to integrate hepatitis testing with other health services, such as HIV and tuberculosis (TB) care. This approach is cost-effective when targeted at high-risk populations and can increase case detection and referrals to specialist care. However, in low-prevalence settings, routine facility-based testing is cost-effective only for high-risk groups. Testing for HBV infection involves serological assays, such as rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) or laboratory-based immunoassays, to detect hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). Laboratory-based assays are preferred in settings with accessible laboratory infrastructure, while RDTs improve access in resource-limited settings. A single serological assay is recommended for initial HBsAg detection, with confirmation using a neutralization step or a second assay if needed. Testing strategies should consider the prevalence of HBsAg in the population and the diagnostic accuracy of the assays used. Further research is needed to simplify testing and care processes and integrate hepatitis services with other health programs.
